Personal Finance: Manage Your Money

Budgeting, an emergency fund, insurance, loans and credit score, goals, retirement, tax planning and fraud safety: how to manage your money well before and while you invest.

Beginner15 topics

1. What personal finance covers

Personal finance means deciding how you earn, spend, save, borrow, protect and grow your money, so that your life goals are paid for and a bad event does not ruin you. It matters more than picking good shares: a person with a modest salary and good habits often ends up wealthier than a high earner who spends everything.

  • Cash flow: knowing what comes in and what goes out each month.
  • Safety: an emergency fund and the right insurance.
  • Debt: borrowing only when it makes sense and repaying it on time.
  • Goals and investing: matching each goal with a suitable investment.
  • Tax and paperwork: keeping more of what you earn, and making sure your family can reach your money.

2. Know where you stand: net worth

Net worth is everything you own minus everything you owe. It is the single best measure of financial progress, far better than salary. Work it out once a year.

Item₹
Savings account and fixed deposits1,50,000
Mutual funds and shares3,00,000
EPF balance4,50,000
Car (current resale value)3,00,000
Total assets12,00,000
Car loan outstanding1,80,000
Credit card balance20,000
Total liabilities2,00,000
Net worth10,00,000

Value assets at what they would sell for today, not what you paid. A car loses value every year, so a loan-funded car can lower your net worth even though it feels like an asset.

3. Make a budget you can follow

A budget is a plan for your money, not a punishment. A simple starting point is the 50/30/20 rule, applied to your take-home pay. Adjust the percentages to your city, family and income.

BucketShareOn ₹60,000 take-homeExamples
Needs50%₹30,000Rent, groceries, bills, school fees, minimum EMIs
Wants30%₹18,000Eating out, shopping, trips, subscriptions
Savings and investing20%₹12,000Emergency fund, SIPs, extra loan repayment

Track your spending for one month using your bank and UPI statements: most people are surprised by what they find. Then pay yourself first: set an automatic transfer to savings and SIPs on the day after your salary arrives, and spend what is left. If EMIs and rent already take most of your income, make increasing that 20% your first goal.

4. Build an emergency fund

An emergency fund is money set aside for job loss, medical bills or urgent repairs. It stops you from breaking investments or borrowing at high interest when something goes wrong. It comes before investing in shares.

  • Size: 3 to 6 months of essential expenses; 6 to 12 months if your income is irregular or you are the only earner.
  • Where: a savings account, a sweep-in fixed deposit or a liquid fund. It should be safe and available within a day or two.
  • Not in: shares, equity funds, gold, or a long lock-in product. These can be down or locked exactly when you need the money.
  • Example: essential expenses of ₹35,000 a month × 6 = ₹2,10,000. Saving ₹10,000 a month gets you there in 21 months.
  • Use it only for real emergencies, and refill it afterwards.

5. Protect yourself with insurance

Insurance exists to protect you from losses you could not pay for yourself. It is a cost for protection, not an investment. Buy these two before you start investing seriously.

  • Term life insurance: if you have dependants, it pays them a large sum if you die during the policy term. A common rule of thumb is cover of 10 to 15 times your annual income, plus your outstanding loans. It is the cheapest way to buy life cover.
  • Health insurance: a hospital stay can wipe out years of savings. Buy your own policy even if your employer covers you, because employer cover usually ends with the job. Check the sum insured, room-rent limits, waiting periods, co-payment and network hospitals.
  • Personal accident cover and vehicle insurance: useful, and third-party motor insurance is mandatory by law.
  • Be careful with products that mix insurance and investing (endowment, money-back and many ULIP plans). They usually give low cover and modest returns. Keeping term insurance and investments separate is normally cheaper and clearer.
  • Disclose your health and habits honestly in the proposal form, and tell your family about the policy. Undisclosed facts are a common reason for rejected claims.

6. Borrow wisely

A loan lets you buy today and pay later, with interest. Some loans can build your future, such as a sensible home or education loan. Others only pay for things that lose value. High-interest debt usually costs more than investments can reliably earn, so repay it before you invest.

  • Keep total EMIs below about 40% of your take-home pay. Lower is safer.
  • Compare the total cost, not just the EMI: a longer tenure lowers the EMI but raises the total interest.
  • Example: ₹10 lakh at 9% for 5 years has an EMI of about ₹20,760, so you repay about ₹12.46 lakh in all. The interest is about ₹2.46 lakh.
  • Repay the costliest debt first (the avalanche method), or the smallest first if quick wins keep you motivated (the snowball method).
  • Lenders cannot charge prepayment penalties on floating-rate loans taken by individuals for non-business purposes, under RBI rules. Prepaying early in a loan saves the most interest.
  • Avoid borrowing to invest, and be careful with instant-loan apps. Check that the lender is an RBI-regulated bank or NBFC.
  • If you stand guarantor for someone, their loan can become your responsibility and can affect your credit score.

7. Credit cards and your credit score

A credit card is useful if you pay the full bill every month: you get interest-free days and rewards. It becomes dangerous when you carry a balance, because interest is often 3% to 4% a month, or roughly 36% to 48% a year.

  • Always pay the total amount due, not the minimum amount due. Set up auto-pay.
  • Example: a ₹50,000 balance at 3.5% a month costs about ₹1,750 in the first month, or about ₹21,000 over a year if the balance stays there, before GST and fees.
  • Your credit score (300 to 900, from bureaus such as CIBIL) tells lenders how you handle credit. Above 750 is generally considered good and can win you lower interest rates.
  • What helps: paying every EMI and card bill on time, using a small share of your card limit (under about 30%), and keeping a long record.
  • What hurts: late payments, settling a loan for less than you owe, and applying for many loans in a short time.
  • You are entitled to a free full credit report once a year from each bureau. Check it for errors and for loans you did not take.

8. Set goals with numbers and dates

'I want to save more' is a wish. 'I need ₹20 lakh in 10 years for my child's education' is a goal you can plan for. Write down each goal, its date and its cost in future money, because prices rise.

When you need the moneyExamplesUsually suitable
Within 3 yearsEmergency fund, vehicle, wedding soonSavings account, fixed or recurring deposit, liquid fund
3 to 5 yearsHouse down paymentDebt funds, fixed deposits, conservative hybrid funds
More than 5 yearsChild's education, retirementMostly diversified equity funds, along with PPF, EPF or NPS

Allow for inflation. At 6% a year, ₹10 lakh of costs today becomes about ₹17.9 lakh in 10 years. And ₹1 lakh kept idle for 20 years buys only what about ₹31,000 buys today. The nearer a goal gets, the more of the money should move to safer options.

9. Why starting early matters so much

Compounding means your returns earn returns of their own. Time is the most powerful part of it, more powerful than the amount or a slightly better return.

₹10,000 a month at 12% a year (illustrative)You investValue at the end
For 10 years₹12 lakhAbout ₹23 lakh
For 20 years₹24 lakhAbout ₹1 crore
For 30 years₹36 lakhAbout ₹3.5 crore

Starting 10 years later does not cost you 10 years of savings: it can cost you most of the final amount. Equity returns are not fixed and 12% is not guaranteed, but the pattern holds for any positive return. Start small now, and increase the amount each time your income rises.

10. Where your money can go

No single product is best. Each one trades off safety, return, access and tax. Rates change, so check the current figures before you decide.

OptionRiskAccessGood for
Savings accountVery lowAny timeDaily money, part of the emergency fund
Fixed or recurring depositLowEarly withdrawal may cost a penaltyGoals within about 3 years
PPFVery low (government-backed)15-year lock-in, partial withdrawal laterLong-term safe savings
EPFVery lowMainly for retirement; partial withdrawals allowedSalaried employees' retirement
NPSDepends on your equity shareMostly locked until age 60Low-cost retirement saving
Debt mutual fundsLow to moderateUsually within days3 to 5 year goals
Equity mutual funds and sharesHigh in the short termUsually within daysGoals more than 5 years away
GoldModerateVaries by formA small share for diversification

Bank deposits are insured by the DICGC up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, which includes interest. Be wary of anyone who offers high returns with no risk: return and risk go together.

11. Plan for retirement

Retirement is the largest goal most people have, and no one will lend you money for it. Your expenses will continue for decades with no salary, and they will rise with inflation.

  • Estimate the amount: ₹50,000 a month of expenses today becomes about ₹2.15 lakh a month in 25 years at 6% inflation, or about ₹25.8 lakh a year.
  • A common rule of thumb is a corpus of 25 to 30 times your annual expenses at retirement: here, about ₹6.4 crore to ₹7.7 crore. Treat it as a rough guide and review it regularly.
  • Use the building blocks: EPF if you are salaried, NPS and PPF for steady saving, and equity funds for long-term growth.
  • Do not withdraw your EPF when you change jobs: transfer it, so it keeps compounding.
  • Do not stop retirement saving to fund children's goals. Education can be funded with loans, retirement cannot.
  • Move part of the money to safer options as you approach retirement, so that a market fall just before you stop working does less damage.

12. Plan your taxes without letting tax lead

Good tax planning means using the rules correctly, not buying a poor product to save tax. Tax rules change often, so verify them each year on incometax.gov.in or with a tax professional.

  • Compare the two regimes every year. The new regime has lower slab rates but allows few deductions; the old regime allows deductions such as those for PPF, EPF, ELSS, life insurance premiums, health insurance and home loan interest. Under Budget 2025 rules, the new regime has no tax on income up to ₹12 lakh after rebate (₹12.75 lakh for salaried people, with the standard deduction).
  • Deductions only help if you use the old regime and they are investments you wanted anyway. Do not buy a poor insurance policy in March just to save tax.
  • File your return on time, even with no tax due. It helps with loans and visas, and is needed to carry forward losses.
  • Check Form 26AS and the Annual Information Statement (AIS) to see what income and TDS are reported in your name.
  • See the Tax Basics module for how gains from shares and mutual funds are taxed.

13. Protect your family's access to your money

Many families in India lose track of money because nobody knew it existed or the paperwork was missing. A little organisation now spares them great difficulty later.

  • Add nominees on every bank account, demat account, mutual fund folio, insurance policy and EPF account.
  • A nominee receives the money, but legal heirs can still claim it under the law. Write a will, especially if you own property or have a complicated family situation.
  • Hold key assets jointly with your spouse where that makes sense.
  • Keep one list of all accounts, policies and loans, and of where passwords are kept, and tell a trusted family member where it is. Never write down actual passwords or OTPs on it.
  • Make sure your spouse or an adult family member knows how to run the household finances.

14. Stay safe from fraud

Fraudsters rely on fear, greed and hurry. Slow down: no genuine bank, police officer or government agency needs you to act in the next five minutes.

  • Never share an OTP, PIN, CVV or password with anyone, including people claiming to be from your bank.
  • You never need to enter your UPI PIN or scan a QR code to receive money. Those actions only send money.
  • 'Digital arrest' calls are a scam. Police and agencies do not arrest people over video calls or ask for money to clear your name.
  • Avoid guaranteed-return schemes, stock tips in WhatsApp or Telegram groups, and fake trading apps. Check that an adviser is registered on the SEBI website.
  • Do not install screen-sharing apps or open APK files at a stranger's request.
  • If you lose money, act at once: call the cybercrime helpline 1930, report at cybercrime.gov.in, and tell your bank. Speed improves the chance of stopping the transfer.
  • For unresolved bank complaints, go to the RBI Ombudsman at cms.rbi.org.in.

15. The order to do things in, and a yearly check-up

If it all feels like too much, follow these steps in order. Each step makes the next one safer.

  • 1. Track your spending and set a budget.
  • 2. Build a small starter emergency fund of about one month's expenses.
  • 3. Get health insurance, and term insurance if anyone depends on you.
  • 4. Pay off high-interest debt such as credit cards and personal loans.
  • 5. Complete your emergency fund of 3 to 6 months.
  • 6. Invest for your goals with SIPs, starting with retirement.
  • 7. Once a year: recalculate net worth, review goals and insurance cover, check your credit report and nominees, compare tax regimes, and increase your SIPs along with your income.

Charts and visuals

Worked examples

A first budget on ₹40,000

Take-home pay is ₹40,000. Rent, food and bills take ₹24,000 (60%), which is above the 50% guide but common in a big city. Wants are cut to ₹8,000 (20%), leaving ₹8,000 (20%) for saving: ₹4,000 to the emergency fund and a ₹4,000 SIP, both set to run automatically on the 2nd of each month.

How much term cover?

Annual income is ₹8 lakh, and there is a ₹15 lakh home loan. At 10 to 15 times income, cover of ₹80 lakh to ₹1.2 crore, plus the ₹15 lakh loan, suggests about ₹1 crore to ₹1.35 crore. Existing investments that the family could use can reduce the figure.

Prepay the loan or invest?

A personal loan at 14% should usually be prepaid first: paying it off is like a guaranteed 14% return, which no safe investment offers. A home loan at 8.5% is a closer choice: many people keep their SIPs running and prepay a little each year, especially if the loan is still in its early years.

Real-life scenarios

Job loss without a cushion

A software engineer with ₹6 lakh in equity funds and no emergency fund loses a job during a market fall of 25%. Needing cash for EMIs, they sell ₹3 lakh of funds at the low. With six months' expenses set aside, they could have left the funds alone until the market recovered.

Employer health cover ends

A 45-year-old relies only on a company health plan. After leaving the job and developing diabetes, a new policy has waiting periods, higher premiums and possible exclusions. Buying a basic personal policy at 30 would have kept cover continuous.

The minimum-due trap

A card user pays only the minimum on a ₹1 lakh balance for a year and keeps spending small amounts. The bill barely falls while interest at about 40% a year adds up. Moving the balance to a cheaper personal loan and stopping card use breaks the cycle.

A call from the 'bank'

A caller knows your name and says your card will be blocked unless you share an OTP. Banks never ask for it. You hang up, call the number on the back of your card, and find nothing wrong. If you had shared it and lost money, the first steps would be 1930 and your bank, immediately.

Use cases

  • Working out your net worth once a year and tracking the trend.
  • Setting automatic transfers for savings and SIPs on the day after salary day.
  • Deciding between prepaying a loan and investing by comparing the interest rate with a realistic after-tax return.
  • Reviewing insurance cover after marriage, a child or a new home loan.
  • Choosing the tax regime each year with real numbers instead of assumptions.

Key takeaways

  • Spend less than you earn, and automate the difference.
  • Emergency fund and insurance come before investing in shares.
  • Clear high-interest debt first; pay credit cards in full every month.
  • Give every goal an amount and a date, and match the investment to the time you have.
  • Start early: time does more for your wealth than almost anything else.
  • Keep nominations and records up to date, and never share an OTP or PIN.

Key terms, explained

Net worth
Everything you own minus everything you owe. The best single measure of your financial progress.
Emergency fund
Cash or very safe, liquid savings to cover 3 to 6 months of expenses. Keep it separate from investments.
Term insurance
Pure life cover that pays a large sum to your family if you die during the policy term, with no return if you survive.
Health insurance
A policy that pays hospital and treatment costs up to the sum insured, subject to its waiting periods and limits.
EMI
Equated monthly instalment: the fixed monthly amount that repays a loan, made up of interest and principal.
Credit score
A number from 300 to 900, from bureaus such as CIBIL, that shows lenders how reliably you repay. Above 750 is generally good.
Compounding
Returns that earn their own returns over time, so growth accelerates.
Inflation
The general rise in prices over time, which reduces what your money can buy.
Asset allocation
How you split money among asset classes such as equity, debt, gold and cash, based on goals and risk.
Diversification
Spreading money across different investments to reduce the damage from any one of them.
SIP
Systematic Investment Plan: investing a fixed amount at regular intervals into a fund.
PPF
Public Provident Fund: a government-backed savings scheme with a 15-year lock-in and an interest rate set each quarter.
EPF
Employees' Provident Fund: retirement savings for salaried employees, with contributions from both employee and employer.
NPS
National Pension System: a low-cost, market-linked retirement scheme, with most of the money locked until age 60.

Questions learners ask

How much of my salary should I save?

Twenty percent of take-home pay is a good target, and more if you started late. If that is not possible yet, start with what you can, even 5%, and raise it with every increment. The habit matters more than the first amount.

Should I invest or clear my loan first?

Clear high-interest debt such as credit cards and personal loans first, since no safe investment reliably beats those rates. For low-interest loans such as a home loan, you can do both, as long as you have an emergency fund and insurance.

Is my employer's health insurance enough?

Usually not. It ends when the job does, and its cover may be small for a family. Buying your own policy while you are young and healthy keeps you covered and reduces the risk of waiting periods or rejection later.

Does checking my own credit score lower it?

No. Checking your own score is a soft enquiry and has no effect. Many hard enquiries from lenders in a short time, when you apply for loans or cards, can lower it.

Are LIC or other endowment policies a good investment?

They provide some guaranteed value, but returns are usually modest and the life cover is often small for the premium. If you are buying a new policy, compare it with a term plan plus a separate investment. If you already hold one, check its surrender value and terms before deciding, since exiting early can be costly.

I earn very little. Does this apply to me?

Yes, and the order of steps matters even more: a small emergency fund and basic health cover protect you from debt. Start with whatever you can save regularly, even ₹500 a month, and avoid high-interest loans.
